doc.title: Onaje Allan Gumbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001

title: Gary McFarland's letter and meeting Herbie Hancock
summary: A televised festival leads Gary McFarland to write him; the faculty opens and posts the letter. He later meets McFarland and Herbie Hancock.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: It was like a stereotype. I don’t want to go there but it seemed like that’s exactly what’s happening. And I was already talked up before I got there. So I said, “Wait a minute I just got here and I’m not sure.” “It’s okay, it’s okay, you’ll be fine.” Needless to say I was in the band, again the only black musician in the whole band. Through that we did a festival at Villanova. And it was televised on PBS. And Gary McFarland watched it and wrote me a letter.
No kidding. I’ll be darned. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -5-

And what happened, at that time we still had a faculty instructor. So in his infinite wisdom, not realizing he had broken all the laws of the postal service, Gary mailed me a letter, right? And it says Attention — you know if you get a letter Attention so-and-so, that is the person that’s supposed to open that letter. And what happened is that the director, his name was Steve Wolczynski, he had introduced me on the air as “the piano player from The Queens.” Because there’s only one borough that says “the” before and that’s The Bronx. For every other borough it’s like Queens, Brooklyn, Manhattan, Staten Island. But you get to “The Bronx” you had “The Bronx.” So he said “The Queens.” So Gary thought that was real funny, because he said “Attention, piano player from The Queens.” Well it came to the jazz department—
Oh he didn’t know your name.
Yeah, he didn’t know my name. Because—

Yeah they didn’t announce it or it just went by real fast. Because we did a composition that I had written that I had never done arranging before either. So they helped me orchestrate this tune and we did it. And so he opened the letter. Not only did he open the letter, he Xeroxed the letter and put the letter on the bulletin board, so everybody could read this letter that was mailed to me. I’m in theory class and they say, “Allan, man” there was a guy, Joe Pizano I think his name was, “there’s a letter for you on the bulletin board.” I said, “What?” I go down and there’s this letter from Gary McFarland. Now mind you I was excited but I didn’t realize the fact that this man has broken all the laws and actually invaded my privacy, because the letter was addressed to me. And I met Gary McFarland, later I went down to New York. And he had had a record label called Sky Records. He, Cal Tjader and Gabor Szabo. Unfortunately all three of them have passed away. So even during school I was starting to get a taste of the professional world. And that kind of culminated with being connected with another person who has been a mentor to me, Billy Taylor. And I guess prior to that Herbie Hancock. Because I met Herbie when an advertising firm came to give a lecture at a job, an ad agency, and one of the people working there was a friend of my sister. So they thought I might like to attend this seminar about music in commercials. And they had shown a commercial, a cigarette commercial, and actually, this is a little trivia, it’s “The Prisoner” by Herbie Hancock, the tune “I Have a Dream” was originally a cigarette commercial tune. It originally was a cigarette commercial. And it was great, I mean the tune is awesome, but that’s where it started. That’s where the gem started. But I went and met one of the people who were doing the lecture. I had a meeting with him and he thought I should meet Herbie. So I went to a concert that Herbie was doing in Central Park and introduced myself to him. And we started to hang out. I started going to his house and everything else, like wow © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -6-
